correctness.rationale: The unrestricted two-seat theorem is proved by the quota-candidate insertion lemma. For odd n, one quota candidate represents more than half the electorate; for even n=2q simultaneous failure of both replacements implies a q-sized cohesive unrepresented group for the original JR pair, contradiction. Starting from any JR two-seat committee, insert a quota candidate and then use a DR reference committee to complete the second seat. Incoming candidates have exactly q supporters, hence every swap is admissible under Definition 27. The three-seat witness directly checks all possible improving swaps, and the m≤k+1 lower bound follows from one-exchange adjacency. The standalone integer verifier completed 149848 low-seat tests and all n≤4,m=4,k=3 profiles. No finite enumeration substitutes for the general argument.

claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: Prior Proposition 29 is existential (there is a k=4 DR-feasible instance with a bad local optimum). It neither covers nor implies universal impossibility for k=2 or existence at k=3 on CI ballots. The result that DR implies local DR does not imply the reverse; the new insertion lemma supplies the missing reverse under k≤2 and feasibility. Earlier JR results only establish feasible JR committees, not this local-to-global reverse.

originality.rationale: Relative to the full text of arXiv:2609.29332v1, which introduced DR and local DR, this contribution proves local/global equivalence for all DR-feasible two-seat instances, with a bound of two admissible improving swaps, and sharp three-seat candidate-interval failure with five candidates. Proposition 29 instead provides a four-seat, 24-voter, seven-candidate counterexample. Indexed semantic searches and accessible prior scientific claim comparison found no equivalent or dominating result. Residual risk: differently phrased or unindexed prior work may exist.

value.rationale: For a recently proposed polynomial-time local fairness algorithm, this establishes exactly where a feasible zero-deviation solution is necessarily recovered by every local optimum. The proof gives a constant two-swap path for arbitrary voter/candidate counts with two seats, while the minimal five-candidate interval counterexample explains why the positive phenomenon breaks with three seats. This is a structural local-to-global boundary, not a computational toy or a restatement of the source’s four-seat example.
